meaning: The number of capable men serving in the house of God
description: The number 1760 appears in 1 Chronicles 9:13, where it indicates the number of priests and Levites who were heads of their fathers' houses – "one thousand seven hundred and sixty, able men for the work of the service of the house of God." The context is the rebuilding of the temple community after the exile in Babylon, where the books of Chronicles carefully document those who returned to resume the holy service. The number underscores the scope and organization of the temple service and testifies that a significant group was devoted to God's house. That these men are described as "able" (Hebrew gibbore ḥayil) points to the fact that temple service required both spiritual dedication and practical competence.

versions.meaning: The number 1760 has no known established symbolic meaning in biblical or Jewish tradition.
versions.description: 1760 is not a number that appears directly in the Bible, nor does it have an acknowledged symbolic role in Jewish numerology (gematria) or traditional biblical symbolism. It can be decomposed mathematically (for example, 10 × 176, where 176 is the number of verses in Psalm 119, the longest psalm), but such a connection is not an established part of biblical or Jewish tradition. The number also holds no prominent place in kabbalistic literature.

The context is the rebuilding of the temple community after the exile in Babylon, where the books of Chronicles carefully document those who returned to resume the holy service. footnotes.text: The Hebrew expression gibbore ḥayil (גִּבּוֹרֵי חָיִל) is often used for military heroes or men of means, but here it is applied to temple servants, underscoring that service in the house of God was regarded as a honorable and demanding task.

Mathematically, 1760 can be decomposed as 10 × 176, where 176 is the number of verses in Psalm 119, the longest chapter in the Bible. However, this connection is not an established part of Jewish or biblical tradition.

1 Chronicles 9 serves as an overview of those who settled in Jerusalem after returning from Babylon and has many parallels with Nehemiah 11. The lists of temple servants show continuity in Levitical service from before to after the exile.
